case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the filing deadline for petitions for review of final orders of removal in immigration cases is jurisdictional or a claims-processing rule subject to equitable exceptions.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(1), the Immigration and Nationality Act's 30-day deadline for filing petitions for review of final orders of removal, as well as broader Administrative Procedure Act provisions governing judicial review of agency decisions.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pierre Riley argues that the 30-day filing deadline under the INA is not jurisdictional in nature but rather a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule that is subject to equitable tolling, waiver, or forfeiture, and that the Fourth Circuit erred in dismissing his petition for lack of jurisdiction rather than treating the deadline as a procedural rule that courts may excuse under appropriate circumstances; Riley further contends that courts should apply the Supreme Court's modern framework distinguishing true jurisdictional requirements from mere claim-processing rules, requiring Congress to clearly and explicitly designate a deadline as jurisdictional before courts treat it as such.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Attorney General Merrick Garland, representing the government, argues that the 30-day deadline for filing petitions for review of removal orders is a strict jurisdictional requirement that strips federal courts of subject-matter jurisdiction when not timely met, that Congress has clearly placed this deadline in a jurisdictional context within the INA's judicial review framework, and that the Fourth Circuit correctly dismissed Riley's untimely petition for lack of jurisdiction without reaching the merits of his immigration claims.
key_precedents: Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center, 568 U.S. 145 (2013) - distinguishing jurisdictional from claims-processing rules
Henderson v. Shinseki, 562 U.S. 428 (2011) - establishing that filing deadlines are not automatically jurisdictional
Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006) - establishing the 'clear statement' rule for jurisdictional designations
Reed Elsevier, Inc. v. Muchnick, 559 U.S. 154 (2010) - further refining jurisdictional vs. non-jurisdictional distinctions
Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007) - holding that statutory time limits for filing notices of appeal are jurisdictional
Zipes v. Trans World Airlines, Inc., 455 U.S. 385 (1982) - treating Title VII filing deadlines as non-jurisdictional
Dada v. Mukasey, 554 U.S. 1 (2008) - addressing equitable considerations in immigration removal proceedings
Stone v. INS, 514 U.S. 386 (1995) - addressing the 30-day petition deadline in immigration proceedings
Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 589 U.S. 221 (2020) - addressing scope of judicial review in immigration cases
Nasrallah v. Barr, 590 U.S. 573 (2020) - addressing judicial review of Convention Against Torture claims
Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, 598 U.S. 411 (2023) - holding that INA's exhaustion requirement is non-jurisdictional
Harrow v. Department of Defense, 601 U.S. 460 (2024) - reaffirming the clear-statement rule for jurisdictional filing deadlines
case_analysis.legal_complexity: Complex - This case sits at the intersection of immigration law, administrative law, and federal courts jurisdiction doctrine, requiring the Court to resolve a circuit split on whether the INA's 30-day petition deadline is jurisdictional, apply evolving Supreme Court jurisprudence distinguishing jurisdictional from claims-processing rules, consider the role of equitable tolling in immigration removal proceedings, and assess the implications of the Convention Against Torture and international human rights law as raised by amici, all while balancing finality interests in immigration adjudication against individual liberty interests in cases involving potential deportation to countries where petitioners may face persecution or torture.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious counterargument by invoking Bowles v. Russell and the structural placement of the deadline within Section 1252's jurisdictional framework, but this argument cannot overcome the clear-statement rule's demand for explicit congressional designation. As Justice Kagan correctly notes, other provisions within Section 1252 do use the word 'jurisdiction' explicitly, which makes the absence of such language in § 1252(b)(1) particularly telling under the negative-implication canon — Congress knows how to speak clearly and chose not to here. Justice Alito's finality concerns are legitimate policy considerations, but Harrow v. Department of Defense teaches that even compelling structural and policy arguments cannot substitute for the clear statement Congress must provide; treating the deadline as a mandatory claims-processing rule still preserves substantial finality interests while allowing courts to address extraordinary circumstances. As Chief Justice, I would assign a narrow opinion holding only that § 1252(b)(1) is a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule, expressly declining to define the full scope of equitable tolling and leaving those contours for lower courts — a minimalist approach that should command the broadest possible coalition while respecting institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: After careful reflection on my colleagues' arguments, I am persuaded to increase my confidence in the Petitioner's position. Justice Kagan's intratextual observation — that Congress used explicit jurisdictional language elsewhere in Section 1252 but conspicuously omitted it from Section 1252(b)(1) — is precisely the kind of textual evidence my originalist and textualist methodology demands, and I cannot dismiss it as mere structural inference. The negative-implication canon, applied rigorously, supports the conclusion that Congress's selective deployment of jurisdictional language within the same statute reflects a deliberate choice. Santos-Zacaria's application of the clear-statement rule to the exhaustion requirement within this very same statutory framework creates a structural parallel I find difficult to distinguish on purely textual grounds, and while Bowles v. Russell remains a legitimate concern, Justice Gorsuch correctly notes that Bowles addressed a court-created extension of a deadline rather than the threshold jurisdictional-characterization question our modern Arbaugh framework governs. I write to emphasize, however, that treating this deadline as a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule does not render it toothless — courts must enforce it rigorously, and equitable tolling should be reserved for genuinely extraordinary circumstances consistent with Congress's evident intent to impose strict finality in immigration proceedings.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: After reviewing my colleagues' arguments in round 2, I find the convergence of textualist reasoning compelling even under my own methodology. Justice Kagan's intratextual observation — that Congress used explicit jurisdictional language elsewhere in Section 1252 but not in Section 1252(b)(1) — is precisely the kind of negative-implication canon argument I cannot dismiss as a textualist without abandoning my own principles. Justice Thomas's movement toward the petitioner position is particularly significant to me: if Justice Thomas, who shares my concern about Bowles v. Russell and structural arguments for jurisdictional force, finds the intratextual evidence sufficient to apply the clear-statement rule here, I must take that seriously. I remain concerned about the practical consequences of equitable tolling in immigration proceedings and would write separately to emphasize that courts should apply tolling only in the most extraordinary circumstances, consistent with the finality interests Congress sought to protect in the 1996 reforms — but my textualist commitments require me to follow where the statutory text leads, and the absence of explicit jurisdictional language in Section 1252(b)(1) against the backdrop of Congress's demonstrated ability to use such language elsewhere is dispositive.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious counterargument — that the structural placement of the 30-day deadline within Section 1252's judicial review framework, combined with Bowles v. Russell's recognition that Congress may impose strict statutory time limits on access to Article III courts, gives the deadline jurisdictional force. But this argument cannot survive Santos-Zacaria's direct application of the clear-statement rule to the very same Section 1252 framework: if the exhaustion requirement in Section 1252(d)(1) is non-jurisdictional despite its mandatory framing and structural placement within the judicial review scheme, the 30-day deadline in Section 1252(b)(1) cannot be jurisdictional absent explicit language Congress conspicuously omitted. Justice Alito's finality concerns are real and I take them seriously — orderly administration of immigration law matters — but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, treating the deadline as a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule does not eliminate its force; it remains mandatory and enforceable, with equitable tolling available only in extraordinary circumstances, which adequately protects finality interests without permanently foreclosing review for vulnerable noncitizens facing persecution based on procedural missteps Congress never clearly designated as jurisdiction-stripping. The human stakes in removal proceedings — where individuals may face torture or death upon return — make it especially important that we not impose jurisdictional bars Congress did not unmistakably enact.

Russell and the structural placement of the deadline within Section 1252's jurisdictional framework, but this argument cannot overcome the clear-statement rule's demand for explicit congressional designation — structural proximity to jurisdictional provisions is precisely what Harrow v. Department of Defense held insufficient. Justice Alito's finality concerns are real, but as Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes, treating the deadline as a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule does not eliminate its force; it remains mandatory and enforceable, with equitable tolling available only in extraordinary circumstances. The textual contrast within Section 1252 itself is dispositive for me: Congress used explicit jurisdictional language in other subsections of Section 1252 but not in (b)(1), and under the canon that Congress acts intentionally in its word choices, that omission speaks volumes. Santos-Zacaria's analysis of the INA's exhaustion requirement within this very same statutory framework is the most directly controlling precedent, and I see no principled basis for treating the 30-day deadline differently when it shares the same textual deficiency.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge to my position by invoking Bowles v. Russell and the structural argument that Congress's placement of the deadline within Section 1252's judicial review framework carries jurisdictional force — but this argument ultimately fails because Bowles addressed a court-created extension of a statutory appellate deadline, not the threshold question of whether Congress clearly designated the underlying deadline as jurisdictional, and our post-Arbaugh framework demands more than structural proximity to jurisdictional provisions. Justice Alito's practical concern about administrative burdens from equitable tolling is not without force, but the answer to that concern is that a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule remains mandatory and enforceable — courts may still dismiss untimely petitions; they simply retain discretion to address extraordinary circumstances rather than being categorically stripped of power. Santos-Zacaria is the most directly controlling precedent: when this Court examined the INA's exhaustion requirement within the very same Section 1252 framework and found it non-jurisdictional despite mandatory framing, it effectively resolved the textual and structural question here, and Stone v. INS — which predates our disciplined jurisdictional jurisprudence — cannot bear the weight the Fourth Circuit placed on it. I am reinforced in my position by the convergence of Justice Kagan's textual observation that other provisions within Section 1252 do use the word 'jurisdiction,' which makes Congress's silence in Section 1252(b)(1) particularly telling under the clear-statement rule.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable consensus, and reviewing my colleagues' arguments in round 2 only reinforces my position. Justice Thomas's movement toward the petitioner — driven by his own textualist methodology recognizing that Congress's selective use of jurisdictional language within Section 1252 itself signals a deliberate omission in § 1252(b)(1) — is particularly significant, as it demonstrates that even the strongest structural counterargument cannot overcome the clear-statement rule's demands. Justice Alito's reluctant concurrence, grounded in his acknowledgment that Santos-Zacaria effectively resolved the textual and structural question for the same statutory framework, confirms that the institutionalist concern I raised — that treating the 30-day deadline differently from the exhaustion requirement in the identical statutory scheme would create doctrinal incoherence — is not merely a policy preference but a genuine legal imperative. I would join Chief Justice Roberts's proposed minimalist approach: hold narrowly that § 1252(b)(1) is a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule, decline to define the full scope of equitable tolling, and leave those contours to lower courts — an approach that preserves the Court's legitimacy while respecting the clear-statement framework our precedents have carefully constructed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious counterargument, contending that the structural placement of § 1252(b)(1) within Congress's comprehensive judicial review framework carries jurisdictional force under Bowles v. Russell's recognition that Congress may strictly police access to Article III courts. However, this structural argument cannot substitute for the clear statement our precedents require — Harrow v. Department of Defense explicitly held that contextual proximity to jurisdictional provisions does not itself supply the requisite clear statement, and Santos-Zacaria applied precisely this logic within § 1252 itself when it held the exhaustion requirement non-jurisdictional despite its placement in the same statutory scheme. Justice Alito's invocation of finality interests and administrative burdens is a policy argument that cannot override the textual and doctrinal framework Arbaugh and its progeny established; Congress remains free to clearly designate the deadline as jurisdictional if it wishes to foreclose equitable tolling, but it has not done so here. The contrast Justice Kagan identifies — that other provisions within § 1252 do use the word 'jurisdiction' while § 1252(b)(1) does not — is textualist evidence I find particularly compelling under my own methodology, as it suggests Congress knew how to speak clearly and chose not to here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge by invoking Bowles v. Russell and the structural placement of § 1252(b)(1) within Congress's jurisdictional grant framework, but as Justice Sotomayor correctly notes, Bowles addressed a court-ordered extension of a statutory appellate deadline — a categorically different situation from the threshold question of whether Congress clearly designated an agency-review petition deadline as jurisdictional in the first instance. The structural proximity argument Justice Alito advances — that placement within § 1252's judicial review scheme supplies sufficient congressional intent — is precisely what Harrow v. Department of Defense rejected: contextual proximity to jurisdictional provisions cannot substitute for the clear statement the Court's modern framework demands. Santos-Zacaria is the most directly controlling precedent here: when this Court examined the INA's exhaustion requirement within the very same § 1252 framework and held it non-jurisdictional for want of explicit jurisdictional language, it effectively resolved the textual and structural question for § 1252(b)(1) as well, since both provisions share the same statutory home and the same textual deficiency. My background as a public defender reinforces what the doctrine already compels — courts should not permanently foreclose merits review of liberty-depriving removal orders through procedural technicalities that Congress never unmistakably designated as jurisdiction-stripping.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Court's modern jurisdictional framework, crystallized through Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp., Henderson v. Shinseki, and most recently Harrow v. Department of Defense, 601 U.S. 460 (2024), demands a clear congressional statement before a filing deadline is treated as jurisdictional rather than a mere claims-processing rule — and 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(1) contains no such explicit jurisdictional designation. The government's reliance on the deadline's placement within the INA's judicial review framework is insufficient under Harrow's teaching that contextual proximity to jurisdictional provisions does not itself supply the requisite clear statement. Santos-Zacaria v. Garland further reinforces this narrow approach by holding that the INA's exhaustion requirement is non-jurisdictional, demonstrating that Congress knows how to speak clearly when it intends jurisdictional consequences and did not do so here. Consistent with my preference for narrow, institutionally cautious rulings, I would hold only that the deadline is a claims-processing rule subject to equitable exceptions, leaving the precise contours of tolling doctrine for lower courts to develop on remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist and textualist, I must examine what Congress actually enacted in 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(1) and the historical understanding of jurisdictional time limits on appellate review. Congress placed the 30-day deadline squarely within the judicial review framework of Section 1252, which has long been understood as a jurisdictional grant and limitation on courts of appeals to review removal orders — this structural placement carries significant weight under a textualist analysis. While I acknowledge the Court's modern clear-statement framework from Arbaugh and its progeny, Bowles v. Russell correctly recognized that congressionally-enacted statutory time limits governing access to Article III courts carry jurisdictional force because Congress, not the courts, defines the scope of appellate jurisdiction under Article III. The movement from an administrative agency to a federal court of appeals is precisely the kind of threshold jurisdictional gateway that Congress may strictly police, and Stone v. INS, though decided before the modern framework crystallized, reflects the longstanding understanding that this deadline is mandatory — an understanding I am reluctant to disturb absent a compelling textual or historical basis for doing so.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: While I acknowledge the Court's modern framework requiring a clear statement before treating a filing deadline as jurisdictional, Section 1252(b)(1) operates within a comprehensive judicial review scheme that Congress deliberately structured to promote finality in removal proceedings, and the structural placement of the 30-day deadline within that framework provides sufficient congressional intent to treat it as jurisdictional. The Bowles v. Russell precedent, though technically limited to Article III court-to-court appeals, reflects the broader principle that Congress may impose strict statutory time limits on access to federal courts, and the INA's removal review framework represents a similarly deliberate congressional choice to cabin judicial intervention. Stone v. INS, 514 U.S. 386 (1995), while perhaps not using 'jurisdictional' in its strictest technical sense as Santos-Zacaria noted, nonetheless reflects longstanding judicial recognition that Congress intended finality in immigration proceedings, and the practical consequences of opening removal orders to equitable tolling arguments would substantially undermine the orderly administration of immigration law that Congress sought to achieve in the 1996 reforms. I am persuaded that the government's interest in finality and the administrative burdens of relitigating stale removal orders counsel against treating this deadline as a mere claims-processing rule subject to equitable exceptions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Court's modern jurisdictional framework, crystallized in Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. and consistently reaffirmed through Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, Harrow v. Department of Defense, and Boechler v. Commissioner, demands a clear congressional statement before a filing deadline is treated as jurisdictional — and Section 1252(b)(1) contains no such explicit jurisdictional designation. Santos-Zacaria is directly controlling: when the Court examined the INA's exhaustion requirement within the very same Section 1252 judicial review framework, it held that the absence of explicit jurisdictional language means the provision functions as a claims-processing rule subject to equitable exceptions, and the same structural and textual analysis applies with equal force to the 30-day petition deadline. The practical consequences for vulnerable noncitizens facing deportation to countries where they may suffer persecution or torture are severe — treating this deadline as a hard jurisdictional bar forecloses merits review entirely based on procedural missteps that may reflect language barriers, lack of counsel, or circumstances beyond a petitioner's control, outcomes fundamentally at odds with the equitable tolling background principle Congress legislates against. Bowles v. Russell is distinguishable because it addressed a court-ordered deadline with explicit statutory grounding in appellate jurisdiction, not an agency-review petition deadline embedded in a comprehensive regulatory scheme where Congress has demonstrated it knows how to use jurisdictional language when it intends to.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Court's modern clear-statement rule, most recently and directly applied in Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, 598 U.S. 411 (2023), requires Congress to unmistakably designate a requirement as jurisdictional before courts treat it as such, and Section 1252(b)(1)'s 30-day deadline contains no such explicit jurisdictional language — a telling contrast with other provisions within Section 1252 that do use the word 'jurisdiction.' Stone v. INS predates the Court's doctrinal clarification in Arbaugh, Henderson, and Santos-Zacaria and addressed a distinct tolling question rather than the jurisdictional character of the deadline itself, making it poor authority for the Fourth Circuit's holding. Filing deadlines are quintessentially non-jurisdictional under our precedents, and Congress legislates against the backdrop of equitable tolling as a traditional feature of American jurisprudence, as Harrow v. Department of Defense reaffirmed; absent a clear statement stripping courts of that equitable power, workability and statutory coherence counsel against treating the deadline as a jurisdiction-stripping provision. Treating the deadline as a claims-processing rule also produces the more administrable and coherent framework, allowing courts to address genuine hardship cases without the harsh all-or-nothing consequences of jurisdictional dismissal in proceedings where liberty and safety interests are at their apex.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Applying the clear-statement rule this Court established in Arbaugh and most recently reaffirmed in Santos-Zacaria and Harrow, Congress must speak clearly before a filing deadline strips federal courts of subject-matter jurisdiction, and Section 1252(b)(1)'s text simply does not contain the explicit jurisdictional designation that rule demands. The plain text of Section 1252(b)(1) reads as an ordinary procedural deadline governing how courts of appeals shall exercise their review authority, not as a limitation on the classes of cases courts may entertain — a structural distinction that matters enormously under our separation-of-powers framework. Stone v. INS, which the Fourth Circuit relied upon, predates this Court's more disciplined jurisdictional jurisprudence and cannot bear the weight placed on it, particularly given that Santos-Zacaria explicitly acknowledged Stone's analytical deficiencies in this precise doctrinal area. Treating this deadline as a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule subject to equitable tolling also better respects the rule of lenity and avoids the harsh consequence of permanently foreclosing judicial review of liberty-depriving removal orders based on procedural technicalities Congress never clearly designated as jurisdiction-stripping.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying the clear-statement rule established in Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. and refined through Henderson v. Shinseki and Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, Section 1252(b)(1)'s 30-day deadline lacks the explicit congressional designation necessary to treat it as jurisdictional rather than a mandatory claims-processing rule. Santos-Zacaria's holding that the INA's exhaustion requirement in Section 1252(d)(1) is non-jurisdictional is directly analogous and effectively abrogates Stone's pre-disciplined-framework reasoning, as both provisions appear in the same statutory scheme and share the same textual deficiency — the absence of clear jurisdictional language. The Ninth and Fifth Circuits correctly recognized that Stone's reasoning is 'clearly irreconcilable' with the Court's modern jurisprudence, and as an institutionalist matter, maintaining a circuit split on a question this Court's own precedents have effectively resolved undermines both judicial consistency and the Court's legitimacy. Treating the deadline as a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule does not eliminate the deadline's force — it remains mandatory and enforceable — but allows courts to address extraordinary circumstances without the harsh and irreversible consequences of a jurisdictional bar in cases involving potential deportation to countries where individuals may face persecution.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the Court's established clear-statement rule from Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. and its progeny, Congress must clearly designate a filing deadline as jurisdictional before courts treat it as stripping subject-matter jurisdiction, and 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(1) does not contain such an explicit jurisdictional designation. The Court's most recent pronouncement in Harrow v. Department of Defense, 601 U.S. 460 (2024), reaffirmed that 'most time bars are nonjurisdictional' even when framed in mandatory terms, and the INA's 30-day deadline, while mandatory, lacks the unmistakable jurisdictional label that Arbaugh and Henderson v. Shinseki require. Furthermore, Santos-Zacaria v. Garland (2023) demonstrates the Court's consistent application of this framework within the INA itself, holding that the INA's exhaustion requirement is non-jurisdictional despite its mandatory framing, which strongly counsels the same conclusion for § 1252(b)(1). Bowles v. Russell is distinguishable because it addressed a court-created extension of a statutory appellate deadline, not the threshold question of whether Congress clearly designated the underlying deadline as jurisdictional in the first instance.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Court's clear-statement rule, firmly established in Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. and most recently applied in Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, requires Congress to explicitly and unambiguously designate a provision as jurisdictional before courts treat it as such — and § 1252(b)(1) simply does not contain that clear statement. As the Ninth and Fifth Circuits correctly recognized post-Santos-Zacaria, the 30-day deadline in § 1252(b)(1) 'suffers from the same flaw' as the exhaustion requirement the Court held non-jurisdictional in Santos-Zacaria: it sits within the same statutory framework, uses no jurisdictional language, and is better understood as a claims-processing rule governing how courts exercise their already-conferred jurisdiction. From a practical standpoint, treating this deadline as a hard jurisdictional bar — particularly in removal cases where individuals may face persecution or torture — produces severe consequences that Congress did not clearly mandate, and my background as a public defender reinforces my conviction that courts should not foreclose merits review through procedural technicalities absent unmistakable congressional direction. Harrow v. Department of Defense (2024) further reaffirms that even filing deadlines require a clear statement to be jurisdictional, and the government cannot satisfy that burden here.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that the INA's comprehensive framework for channeling judicial review reflects a deliberate congressional choice to give these deadlines significant weight, and that treating them as mere claim-processing rules would invite endless tolling litigation. This is not a frivolous concern, and I take seriously the government's interest in finality of removal orders. However, Justice Alito's argument ultimately proves too much: the question is not whether Congress values finality, but whether Congress clearly designated this particular deadline as jurisdictional, and our precedents from Arbaugh through Harrow demand an explicit statement to that effect. Justice Barrett's textual observation is particularly compelling — Congress demonstrated it knows how to strip courts of jurisdiction by using 'no court shall have jurisdiction' language in § 1252(b)(9), and its silence in § 1252(b)(1) is telling under the negative-implication canon. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with instructions to write narrowly on the jurisdictional question alone, expressly reserving the equitable tolling question, which would preserve the Court's institutional credibility by avoiding sweeping pronouncements while still resolving the circuit split on the jurisdictional characterization.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable consensus, and even Justice Alito — whose structural and finality arguments I took most seriously — has acknowledged that the textual evidence under our clear-statement framework does not support the jurisdictional reading. My originalist methodology compels the same conclusion: the original public meaning of 'jurisdictional' requires explicit congressional designation, and as Justice Barrett correctly identifies, Congress demonstrated in § 1252(b)(9) that it knows precisely how to strip courts of jurisdiction using unmistakable language, making its silence in § 1252(b)(1) texturally dispositive rather than ambiguous. Justice Alito's remaining concern about finality and administrative burden is a legitimate policy argument, but under my textualist discipline, policy preferences — however well-founded — cannot supply the clear statement that Congress itself omitted, and it is not this Court's role to infer jurisdictional consequences from statutory structure when Congress has shown it can speak plainly. I write separately to emphasize that this holding flows directly from the original public meaning of jurisdictional limitations and the negative-implication canon, not merely from modern clear-statement doctrine, and to note that Congress retains full authority to impose an explicit jurisdictional bar if it chooses to do so.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Having now heard from all eight colleagues, I find the convergence of textualist reasoning compelling enough to solidify my position. Justice Barrett's core observation — that Congress used explicit 'no court shall have jurisdiction' language in § 1252(b)(9) but conspicuously omitted it in § 1252(b)(1) — is a textual argument I cannot dismiss as a committed textualist, and Auburn Regional's rejection of proximity-based jurisdictional inference directly forecloses the structural argument I initially found persuasive. Justice Thomas reinforces my own methodology against me: substituting inferred congressional purpose for actual statutory text is precisely what textualism prohibits, and my concern about finality, while legitimate as policy, cannot supply the clear statement our precedents demand. I maintain residual concern that treating this deadline as a mere claim-processing rule will generate substantial equitable tolling litigation that burdens immigration courts, but I acknowledge that concern is properly addressed through rigorous application of equitable tolling doctrine rather than through a jurisdictional bar Congress never explicitly imposed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that the INA's comprehensive framework for channeling judicial review reflects a deliberate congressional choice to impose strict procedural requirements, and that treating filing deadlines as mere claim-processing rules subject to equitable tolling would undermine finality in removal proceedings. Justice Barrett's point is particularly compelling — when Congress has demonstrated it knows how to write jurisdictional bars, the absence of such language in an adjacent provision is dispositive, not merely suggestive. The real-world consequences Justice Alito invokes — finality and administrative efficiency — are legitimate interests, but they are properly addressed through the claim-processing rule framework itself, which allows courts to enforce deadlines while preserving equitable exceptions for the most compelling circumstances, rather than through a categorical jurisdictional bar that forecloses all relief for vulnerable petitioners facing persecution.
